articles.title: Verstappen saca el dedo a Hamilton y casi chocan a lo 2021
articles.standfirst: Max creyó que Hamilton le había arruinado una vuelta y se intentó tomar venganza de forma un tanto pendenciera
articles.summary: Max creyó que Hamilton le había arruinado una vuelta y se intentó tomar venganza de forma un tanto pendenciera
articles.body: En cierto que las velocidades no son las mismas que otros años y que se nota que el motor térmico no se basta del todo para ver aquellas puntas de más de 350 km/h en Monza. Piastri marcó 337 km/h como máxima en los Libres 3 del GP de Italia. Pero sigue siendo un circuito al límite, bajando marcha en la doble de Lesmo, donde entra el freno motor y controlar el coche es muy complicado, como en la reducción de la Variante Ascari, con sus tres pianos. Checo tuvo problemas al salir de Lesmo, levantó una nube de polvo y arruinó la vuelta buena de Hamilton en esos libres 3, aunque luego dio otras que le sirvió para ser segundo. Y Max llegaba por detrás y creyó que el que le había fastidiado era Lewis... Se quejó por la radio diciendo: "Otra vez el Ferrari, Dios mío". Pero ahí no acabó la cosa. Unos giros después, cuando ya no estaban en vuelta rápida, Verstappen y Hamilton llegaron emparejado en la curva 1, la Primera Variante, donde se intentó colar por dentro, echando al británico. Y fue cuando casi se tocan. El pasaje de 2021, cuando el de Red Bull quedó montado sobre el halo y con la rueda tocando el casco amarillo de Lewis, regresó de inmediato a la mente de los aficionados. Los comisarios tomaron nota y ambos debieron pasar por comisarios para dar explicaciones, pero era algo completamente innecesario y un tanto pendenciero, por parte del holandés, al que le hirvió la sangre como en tiempos no tan lejanos.

articles.title: Kimi Antonelli becomes first Italian to lead F1 championship into Monza GP since 1953, carries Italy’s hopes and revives a dream last seen with Alberto Ascari

articles.body: For decades, Italian Formula 1 fans have dreamed of seeing one of their own arrive at Monza with the world championship within reach. In 2026, that wait finally ended. Andrea Kimi Antonelli heads into the Italian Grand Prix as the Formula 1 World Championship leader, becoming the first Italian driver in 73 years to occupy the top spot in the standings ahead of his home race. The last to do it was Ferrari great Alberto Ascari in 1953.At just 20, Antonelli has already turned what was supposed to be a promising young career into one of the defining stories of the 2026 F1 season. Driving for Mercedes, the Bologna-born driver has won six Grands Prix and leads the championship with 242 points, 59 clear of his teammate George Russell and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, both on 183.73 years after Ascari, Italy has its championship leaderThe name Alberto Ascari remains synonymous with Italian Formula 1 greatness. Driving for Ferrari, Ascari won consecutive world championships in 1952 and 1953. In 1953, he arrived at the Italian Grand Prix leading the Drivers' Championship, a feat no Italian had repeated at their home race until Antonelli's breakthrough this year.The parallel is particularly striking because Ascari's 1953 season ended with him finishing the championship as world champion, despite retiring from the Italian Grand Prix at Monza.Now, 73 years later, another Italian has arrived at Monza carrying the country's championship hopes. The difference is that Antonelli is doing it in a Mercedes rather than a Ferrari.The 'Kimmy effect' takes over ItalyAntonelli's rise has sparked a new wave of enthusiasm around Italian motorsport. His emergence gives the country's fans something they have rarely had in the modern F1 era: an Italian driver capable of competing for the biggest prize in the sport.And he has done it quickly. After making his F1 debut with Mercedes in 2025 as Lewis Hamilton's replacement, Antonelli has exploded into title contention in his second season. His 2026 campaign already includes six victories and six pole positions from 12 Grands Prix.His success has also created an unusual dynamic at Monza. The Italian Grand Prix traditionally revolves around Ferrari and its passionate Tifosi. This year, however, the home crowd has another driver to cheer for, even though he is wearing Mercedes colours. That makes Antonelli's story different from those of previous Italian favourites. He does not need to drive a Ferrari to become a national sporting icon.From Hamilton's replacement to championship leaderThe expectations surrounding Antonelli were enormous from the moment Mercedes promoted him.He was only 18 when the team handed him Hamilton's seat following the seven-time world champion's move to Ferrari. Mercedes had effectively placed one of the sport's biggest responsibilities on the shoulders of a teenager.Antonelli responded with three podiums and 150 points in his rookie season. The second year has been a completely different story. He has established himself as the driver to beat, winning six races and building a substantial championship advantage. The irony is difficult to ignore: Hamilton, the man Antonelli replaced at Mercedes, is now one of his closest championship rivals, and is driving for Ferrari.Monza presents a very different challengeAntonelli's historic weekend will not be straightforward. A power-unit change means the championship leader is set to start the Italian Grand Prix from the back of the grid, turning what could have been a straightforward homecoming into a recovery mission.Rather than allowing the penalty to overwhelm him, Antonelli has said it takes some pressure away and gives him the chance to enjoy his home race. That could make Sunday's contest even more compelling. The championship leader will have to fight his way through the field at one of the fastest circuits on the calendar while Ferrari drivers Hamilton and Charles Leclerc chase glory in front of their home fans.Mercedes teammate Russell, meanwhile, has already shown strong pace at Monza, topping Friday's second practice session and cutting into the attention surrounding Antonelli.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.summary: Gran Q1 de Carlos, que dejó fuera a Tsunoda y Albon, con coches iguales o superiores y saldrá 14º en parrilla
articles.body: Uno de los detalles del sábado en el GP de Italia lo ha dejado Carlos Sainz, que con tres vueltas con tres juegos nuevos del compuesto blando, logró pasar a la Q2, dejando fuera a Tsunoda, con todo un RB (con el que su compañero Lindblad fue quinto) y a su compañero en Williams, Alex Albon. Sainz ya sabe lo que es llevarse la pole en Italia, la que logró en 2023 por delante de Leclerc y ha mostrado que con un FW-48 que le daba algunas opciones en recta, le ha sacado todo el rendimiento. Además, su mejor vuelta no fue la del rebufo, algo que no le gusta demasiado, por lo que logró el crono en solitario en el segundo intento de la manga. En la Q2, Carlos superó a Ocon y obtuvo el 15º tiempo, pero con la sanción de Antonelli partirá 14º en la carrera, con opciones de una carrera sólida y de poder buscar los puntos de nuevo. Por su parte, Fernando Alonso superó a Stroll para ser el 21º en tiempos y el 20º en la parrilla, pues Kimi Antonelli deberá salir por detrás por el cambio de unidad de potencia. No pudo luchar con los Cadillac, por esa falta de potencia.

articles.title: Top owner Mike Repole sounds off on issues with horse racing leadership
articles.summary: As one of horse racing's most prominent and successful owners, Mike Repole isn't shy about sharing his opinions and gripes about the sport he loves.
articles.body:
SARATOGA SPRINGS - Mike Repole isn't one to let his soapbox go to waste.

As one of horse racing's most prominent and successful owners, Repole, a 57-year-old Queens native who made his fortune (an estimated $2.5 billion, according to Forbes) in the food and beverage industry, isn't shy about sharing his opinions - especially about the state of the sport he loves.

Because as committed as he is to the sport, Repole - the self-proclaimed "commissioner" of horse racing - has serious concerns about where the thoroughbred game is headed.

He addressed them in an interview with the Times Union at Saratoga Race Course this past Friday, the day before Renegade, whom he co-owns with Robert and Lawana Low, raced to an eighth-place finish in the Travers Stakes .

"If things don't change," Repole said, "I think in 10 years the sport's in serious, serious trouble."

Considering that, when Repole sees an issue he feels needs to be addressed, he's not shy about raising his voice or who his opinions might offend.

"I think that there aren't enough vocal people in this sport," he said, "and I think that there's things that, for some reason, people are afraid to say about the sport."

What Repole, who also serves as a co-owner and director of business operations for the United Football League, wants is for the varying track operators, racing regulators and national organizations to come together in some centralized form, with a figurehead in place to oversee it.

"This is a sport that it's probably the only big sport that doesn't have a commissioner - other than myself, by the way," he said. "I think that if there was more infrastructure and a little bit more of the of the big entities that that affect the sport working together - whether it was NYRA and Churchill (Downs), whether it was the breeding farms, whether it was the Jockey Club, whether it was the bigger owners and the bigger trainers - and really look at the sport in its totality, I think it'd be better."

What Repole isn't a fan of is the Horseracing Integrity and Safety Authority. The organization, empowered by an act of Congress, regulates racing in around two dozen states with a focus on racetrack safety and anti-doping and medication rules.

Repole said that he's "not a fan of government or federal involvement." Horse racing is, in his words, "a very hard sport to police," and HISA "really needs an overhaul and change in order for it to work."

"The safety of the sport should have been a priority for the last 120 years," he said. "Knowing what you know, that you couldn't come up with a solution internally to make the sport safer, cleaner, and better for everyone involved, and most importantly, the horse, that's the shame."

In a statement to the Times Union, a HISA spokesperson said: "We agree (the sport is hard to police), which is exactly why a fragmented, state-by-state regulatory system was not sufficient. HISA was created following a bipartisan act of Congress, signed into law by President Trump, to establish national standards and consistent oversight for a sport that previously operated under a patchwork of different rules and enforcement practices.

"HISA is not static, and we will continue to improve and evolve our programs based on data, science and input from those who work in the sport. But returning to the fragmented system that preceded HISA would not make racing safer, fairer or easier to regulate. The answer to the challenges of regulating this sport is to continue strengthening consistent, nationwide standards - not to abandon them."

Repole's gripes with HISA came into full focus recently with numerous posts on social media criticizing the organization and its handling of a scandal involving Marshall Gramm, an owner and prominent horseplayer. Gramm recently agreed to a provisional suspension banning him from ownership and racetrack activities after he was charged with violating HISA rules for allegedly accessing confidential veterinary treatment records through HISA's informational portal.

Repole isn't the only one raising his voice about HISA. On the same day he spoke with the Times Union, Churchill Downs Incorporated CEO Bill Carstanjen sent a letter to the Federal Trade Commission to "express serious concern" about HISA's "significant questions about the governance, transparency, technology controls, and accountability."

Horse Racing Nation obtained and published the letter, which cited both the recent "Fair Hill Five" betting coup scandal involving races at Saratoga and Monmouth Park, as well as the Gramm controversy, and requested that the FTC initiate an independent review of HISA's handling of the matters.

Among those copied on the letter was U.S. Rep. Paul Tonko, the Amsterdam Democrat and lead sponsor of the legislation that empowered HISA.

HISA isn't the only target of Repole's barbs. The Jockey Club, which has been one of the most powerful organizations in American thoroughbred racing for more than 130 years, is also in his crosshairs.

"To me, it's a failure by the Jockey Club, but more importantly, I think it was to their benefit to put (HISA) on," Repole said. "Remember, they're the ones that pushed for HISA. They're the ones that wrote the bylaws, and they're the ones that still have data with them and share data with them. I think they're as responsible for what's going on as HISA."

In a statement to the Times Union, a spokesperson for The Jockey Club, "The Jockey Club was an early supporter of federal legislation to establish national integrity and safety standards for horse racing," noting that it was one of several entities that had "substantive input into the final bill language," including the Breeders' Cup, Churchill Downs, National Thoroughbred Racing Association, United States Anti-Doping Agency, American Association of Equine Practitioners and Humane Society of the United States.

The statement continued, "Supporting the creation of HISA is not the same as controlling HISA. HISA was deliberately established as an independent organization in accordance with the Horseracing Integrity and Safety Act of 2020 and is responsible for its own operations, regulatory decisions, technology, software, and security. Neither The Jockey Club nor its affiliated companies designed, developed, tested, secured, or maintained the HISA Portal or HISA's internal technology systems. The Jockey Club also has no role in setting, reviewing, or testing HISA's controls over data provided to it."

Along with his problems with the way the sport is overseen, Repole is concerned about the sport's declining foal crop and that smaller breeders, owners and horseplayers may be pushed out of what he perceives as a top-heavy environment.

"I was a small owner before I became a big owner," he said. "I was a small horse player before I became a big horse player, and I think it would be a shame if the game shut them out. And I would be really concerned about the future of the game if the smaller players can't play.

He's concerned that horse racing "had a 100-year head start on gambling, and we wasted it," and that even though he wants a younger generation to become invested in the sport, he's not sure that it's a product ready to be marketed to that audience.

The marketing guru wants to see the sport's internal issues fixed first.

"One of the biggest bonds I have with my daughter is horse racing," Repole said. "She's 11 years old. When she's 51 in 40 years, I want to make sure she takes her kids here. I'm definitely concerned about the future of the sport."

articles.title: Italian Grand Prix: Pierre Gasly beats George Russell to stunning Monza pole
articles.summary: Alpine driver Pierre Gasly takes a stunning pole position at the Italian Grand Prix, ahead of Mercedes' George Russell.
articles.body:
Alpine driver Pierre Gasly took a stunning pole position at the Italian Grand Prix.

The Frenchman, whose sole Formula 1 victory came at this race for Red Bull's junior team in 2020, beat Mercedes' George Russell by 0.060 seconds.

McLaren's Oscar Piastri was third but was later given a three-place grid penalty for impeding Liam Lawson in the Red Bull.

The Australian's penalty moves up the Ferraris of Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton, who originally qualified fourth and fifth, and Red Bull's Max Verstappen.

The other McLaren of Lando Norris was only ninth after a messy session for the world champion.

Championship leader Kimi Antonelli of Mercedes qualified seventh but will start at the back because of a grid penalty for taking a new engine.

Gasly's pole comes a day after he lost his third place from the Monaco Grand Prix because the FIA Court of Appeal reinstated a penalty he was given at the race in June.

Saturday's unexpected performance makes him the first Frenchman to take pole for a grand prix since Jean Alesi for Benetton at this race in 1997.

The result is a hiccup for Russell, who has a golden opportunity to make up ground on team-mate Antonelli, who has a 30-place grid penalty.

Antonelli was employed for much of the session in front of Russell to give him a tow, so to be beaten by an Alpine and be only 0.12secs ahead of Piastri was a disappointment.

Russell said he started his final lap too close to Verstappen, who let Antonellli by before the start of it to avoid running in clean air.

"Going into Parabolica, Max just slammed on the brakes and didn't want to be the lead car," Russell said. "In hindsight, it would probably have been better not trying this, but P2 is a good place to start."

Alpine put a large upgrade on their car at the last race in the Netherlands, where Gasly could qualify only 11th. This result came out of nowhere.

How to follow Italian Grand Prix on the BBC

The 30-year-old said: "It was amazing. Thank you to everyone. It was an incredible qualifying. From the first lap in Q1, I felt very good in the car, trying to chip away a bit every single session.

"It felt like a very good lap. It has been nine years trying to chase a pole position and to take my first win here and then my first pole here is amazing."

Russell, who had been a strong favourite for pole in the light of Antonelli's penalty, said: "Firstly, massive congrats to Pierre because that's an incredible performance.

"We were finishing a game of chess 15 minutes before qualifying and he beat me there and I thought, 'well, I will beat him in qualifying.' But here we are. I am disappointed not to be on pole but Pierre was very fast from Q1."

Having already blocked Lawson, Piastri then inadvertently compromised Norris' final run. He was leading the pack around, with Norris behind him, and locked up into the first chicane, going straight on into the run-off area and hampering his team-mate.

Now without a slipstream, Norris was 0.4secs down at the first sector and bled time through the lap. "Without a slipstream, with our straight-line deficiency, it's hard to put something good together," said the Briton.

Ferrari had looked set to be in the mix at the front before qualifying with their new engine that was believed to be worth about 0.1secs per lap.

Hamilton made it through into the final session by only 0.001secs as Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto just failed to displace him, and let out an expletive over the radio when he saw the narrow escape.

And the red cars were just not fast enough in the final session. Leclerc was fourth on both his runs, while Hamilton, ninth on his first run, improved on his second but ended up 0.007secs behind his team-mate.

Gasly says pole 'exceeded all our expectations'

Pole is an extraordinary story for Gasly, who lives in nearby Milan and spoke in Italian to the crowd in the trackside interviews afterwards.

He has laboured in F1's midfield throughout his career, even when he had his big chance at the Red Bull team in 2019. He was dropped back to the junior team, then called Toro Rosso, after half a season, and has been trying to rebuild his career ever since.

A move to Renault-owned Alpine in 2023 offered him a chance at a factory team, but they have struggled badly through most of his time with the team, and finished last in 2025.

Executive adviser Flavio Briatore, who has caused controversy off track this weekend, persuaded Renault to curtail their F1 engine programme at the end of last year and switch to customer Mercedes power-units.

The move, combined with switching off any effort on their 2025 car so as to be as well prepared as possible for this year's new rules, vaulted them towards the head of the midfield.

A strong start to the season was followed by them falling backwards somewhat as others upgraded their cars.

The new parts in Zandvoort did not have an especially auspicious debut, but Gasly has looked strong all weekend. Even so, not even they thought they were in a position to take a pole on merit in Monza.

"It exceeded all our expectations," Gasly said.

articles.title: Sainz: "Ha sido una de esas veces"
articles.standfirst: Saldrá 14º en Monza, tras dejar atrás a Ocon, Tsunoda y Albon, en una gran calificación
articles.summary: Saldrá 14º en Monza, tras dejar atrás a Ocon, Tsunoda y Albon, en una gran calificación
articles.body: Carlos Sainz volvió a disfrutar sobre el Williams, aunque fuera en el nivel limitado que le permite su actual coche. Pasó de forma brillante la Q1, a 1.004 del mejor tiempo de Gasly y luego dejó atrás en la Q2 a Ocon, para llevarse el 15º tiempos y la posición 14ª en la parrilla de salida del GP de Italia. "En nuestros mejores días, a veces logramos colarnos en la Q2, superando quizás a uno de los coches de la zona media. Creo que fue una de esas veces en la Q1, con una buena vuelta, y luego otra buena vuelta en la Q2 para vencer a Ocon. Así que, creo que logré el máximo. Nuestras pequeñas victorias, llegar a la Q2 y superar a un coche en la Q2, es todo lo que tenemos ahora mismo, hasta que mejore", resumía un Sainz serio pero satisfecho. Carlos relataba un problema en la Parabólica durante la Q1. "Sí, iba al límite. En esa vuelta, tuve un buen rebufo de Charles en la curva 1, pero luego pasé el resto de la vuelta sin rebufo, lo que significa que sin rebufo, eres mucho más rápido en curva, pero luego eres muy lento en las rectas, y en esa vuelta tuve que hacer todo en Parabólica para recuperar todo el tiempo que estaba perdiendo en las rectas. De hecho, sí, esa fue mi mejor Parabólica, pero no pude superar mi tiempo, porque luego el resto de las vueltas estuve en rebufo, y nuestro coche en rebufo, a alta velocidad, no es divertido, pero sí esa vuelta es la vuelta que me dejó en la Q1, así que estuvo bien", decía sobre su intento al límite. La carrera, con el turbo de este año, puede ser un pequeño caos el domingo en Monza. "Creo que depende de la disciplina de cada uno al usar el turbo. Creo que todo se reduce a cuánto tiempo de carrera estás dispuesto a perder al entrar en un juego del 'yo-yo' con el turbo, y cuánto tiempo en el modo óptimo quieres mantenerte sin usarlo y simplemente dejar que el sistema lo dicte. Así que va a ser bastante importante dependiendo de quién esté a tu alrededor y quién esté dispuesto a entrar en una batalla de "yo-yo", pronosticaba Sainz. Sainz no estaba sorprendido por la influencia de los rebufos en esta edición en Monza. "No, creo que nuestra simulación ya sugería que el rebufo sería muy potente porque estamos en un coche de F1 con 400-500 CV a mitad de la recta, con mucha resistencia, así que obviamente el rebufo tiene un efecto enorme", reconocía. Carlos evaluaba la experiencia del piloto con estos coches hibridos en el Templo de la Velocidad. "Creo que claramente no es tan bueno como solía ser, creo que especialmente en los lugares donde estamos corriendo sin batería para guardarla para la recta. En la curva 6, la curva 7, las curva 8, esas curvas de velocidad media ahora estamos conduciendo mucho más lento sin despliegue (eléctrico), lo que tal vez esté haciendo que la entrada a esas curvas sea menos desafiante. Y en las rectas, simplemente limitando la velocidad allí a 305-310 donde la estamos limitando, fue un poco extraño", cerraba ante la prensa internacional.

articles.title: Sainz y Alonso escalan en la parrilla de Monza por las penalizaciones
articles.standfirst: Por el momento, Carlos arranca 13º en el GP de Italia y Fernando 18º
articles.summary: Por el momento, Carlos arranca 13º en el GP de Italia y Fernando 18º
articles.body: Los cambios de motor de Antonelli, Albon y Lawson, permiten subir posiciones a los dos pilotos españoles en el GP de Italia de F1. Tras aplicar las penalizaciones, Sainz ganará dos puestos y partirá 13º, muy cerca de los puestos de puntos. Él creía incluso que arrancaba 14º ante la prensa y las televisiones, pero la FIA pasaba la previsión de la parrilla, antes de la investigación de Piastri por obstaculizar a un contrario. En el caso de Fernando Alonso, su ganancia era mayor, pues pasaba a KImi, al de RB y a Albon, al que Sainz había ganado en la Q1. Así, el asturiano arrancará 18º en lugar de 21º, que esa su tiempo de qualy por delante de Lance Stroll. Para la carrera, lo normal es que el flamante y merecido poleman, Pierre Gasly, tenga problemas en los primeros compases con los lobos que llegan por detrás, pero no se le puede descartar para conseguir el podio o la victoria en Monza, una pista en la que logró su primera y único triunfo en 2019, aunque aquel día sin cambiar gomas en toda la carrera por una bandera roja, para disgusto de carlos Sainz que la mereció con McLaren. Se avecina una prueba plagada de adelantamientos basados en la energía eléctrica, para algunos artificiales y para otros, una nueva habilidad para ciertos pilotos. La posible remontada de Antonelli desde el 20º es uno de los alicientes de este domingo en una de las catedrales del automovilismo.

articles.title: Italian GP Qualifying: Pierre Gasly claims shock first pole position to beat George Russell to head of Monza grid for Alpine
articles.summary: Alpine's Pierre Gasly upstages the title contenders to deliver his first pole in F1 after almost 200 races; Mercedes' George Russell second with Ferraris promoted by Oscar Piastri penalty; watch the Italian GP live on Sunday at 2pm (build-up from 12.30pm) on Sky Sports F1
articles.body:
A day after losing his podium finish from June's Monaco Grand Prix for a second time after a court ruling, Gasly was unexpectedly a threat at the front throughout qualifying at high-speed Monza.

The Frenchman was third on the timesheet heading into the final Q3 runs before saving his best until last to usurp provisional polesitter George Russell and take the coveted top spot with a surging final lap of 1:21.786.

Gasly's first pole in F1, for his 190th race, comes six years after he claimed what stands as his sole career win, also at Monza, which was achieved in similarly unlikely circumstances for AlphaTauri.

It is the first pole position in F1 for the Alpine name and a first for the Renault-owned Enstone team since 2009.

Russell was left to rue a "messy" start to his final lap behind Red Bull's Max Verstappen and he missed out on pole by 0.060s.

But the Briton still starts on the front row in second for a race in which championship-leading team-mate Kimi Antonelli will start among the grid's back rows due to engine-change penalties.

Antonelli, who helped Russell with a tow during qualifying, took seventh but always knew he would drop to the back wherever he qualified.

McLaren's Oscar Piastri qualified third but was handed a three-place grid penalty after the session for blocking Red Bull's Liam Lawson in Q2.

Piastri drops to sixth on Sunday's grid as a result with Ferrari's Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton promoted to third and fourth respectively, with Verstappen into fifth.

Both Ferraris will now start on the second row despite a difficult qualifying session in which their expected pole-contending pace never materialised.

Indeed, the Scuderia had been fortunate to get both cars into the top 10 at all after Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto finished just 0.001s behind 10th-fastest Hamilton at the end of Q2. Leclerc had been ninth.

After consecutive poles and race wins either side of the summer break, reigning champion Lando Norris qualified only ninth.

The Briton was shorn of a tow on his final lap of Q3 after a Piastri error at the first chicane in front of him, although moves up to eighth on the grid owing to Antonelli's penalties.

With the championship leader dropping to the back, Gasly's Alpine team-mate Franco Colapinto takes over seventh with Norris eighth and Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad ninth. Bortoleto ends up 10th.

Gasly delivers qualifying shock for the ages at the Temple of Speed

After the frustration of Friday - when Gasly and Alpine learned from the FIA's International Court of Appeal that his pit-lane speeding penalties from June's Monaco race would be reapplied and so he would drop from third to seventh in a result revised for the second time - the prospect of them delivering such an eye-catching response on track would have appeared far-fetched.

Alpine are enjoying a much-improved season compared to 2025, when they finished last in the standings, but until Saturday had not started a race higher than seventh on the grid.

Gasly was ninth fastest in the day's earlier final practice session, six tenths of a second off Russell's benchmark pace, but their Mercedes-engined A526 car was suddenly a pole contender in the Frenchman's hands come qualifying.

With Alpine appearing to have trimmed out the car's rear-wing levels for F1's fastest track, Gasly led the way in Q1 before showing that was no fluke by finishing fourth-fourth in Q2 and still ahead of pole favourite Russell.

The first runs of Q3 then underlined that Gasly was a serious contender. Russell set the quickest time but Gasly remained right in the mix in third, just 0.072s behind.

The final run then played out absolutely perfectly for the Alpine driver. While Piastri blew his pole chance by locking up into the first chicane, and Russell's warm-up for his final attempt was compromised, Gasly seized his chance and jumped ahead of both.

Confirmation of pole triggered scenes of jubilation in the Alpine garage, with an emotional Gasly shouting on team radio: "Yessssss! Let's go. I've been waiting for that one!"

Reflecting on the achievement in his post-qualifying interview, the Frenchman said: "From the first lap in Q1, I felt very good in the car. I tried to chip away a little bit, every single session, and it felt like a very good lap.

"It's been nine years trying to chase the opportunity to get a pole.

"I won my first race in Monza and got my first pole at this track. It's something special around here."

Russell paid tribute to Gasly, revealing that the Frenchman had also beaten him at chess ahead of qualifying.

"Massive congrats to Pierre. That's an incredible performance," said Russell.

"We were finishing a game of chess about 15 minutes before qualifying and he beat me there and I went 'well, I think I will beat you in qualifying' and here we are, he's ahead of me again!

"Huge congrats to him. I was disappointed to not get pole position. It was a bit messy with Verstappen opening the lap, I did the lap very close, but Pierre and Alpine have been super fast."

Gasly is the first Frenchman to claim pole position in the sport since Jean Alesi for Benetton - one of the forerunners of the Alpine team - at Monza in 1997.

articles.title: Alonso mira al futuro: "No me da estrés este año, la determinación es tener un mejor 2027"
articles.standfirst: El asturiano cuenta los medios desplazados, con MARCA presente, las dificultades vividas en Monza y las tareas a cumplir
articles.summary: El asturiano cuenta los medios desplazados, con MARCA presente, las dificultades vividas en Monza y las tareas a cumplir
articles.body: Fernando Alonso llegó a Monza con un pesimismo reinante que la pista italiana confirmó. Ni es entretenida en el coche. "Ya no es un templo de la velocidad. En Barcelona íbamos a 360, en Budapest a 355... y aquí a 312", comentó. Y el Aston Martin no puede dar más de lo que da. Sólo superó a Lance Stroll, tampoco fue la clasificación ideal y partirá 19º al aprovechar las sanciones de Kimi Antonelli, Liam Lawson y Alex Albon. El objetivo sólo puede ser sacar la caña de pescar y esperar a circuitos mejores. Pero a Alonso no le cambia la vida. Y mira al futuro, aunque el suyo no está del todo claro. "Habrá mejores circuitos que otros, pero estamos al fondo de la parrilla y no me da estrés este año. Si hay oportunidad de sumar otro punto, bien. Pero no cambia la mentalidad y determinación de tener un mejor 2027", comentó ante la prensa desplazada, con MARCA presente. Vuelven las interpretaciones sobre la mesa, aunque su discurso es el de unión. "No estamos en la posición que queremos como equipo, hay una montaña que escalar… Pero en el chasis encontramos la forma de mejorar para el año que viene y necesitamos lo mismo en el motor", añadió. Las dos dimensiones del AMR26. El chasis está y es bueno. "Es muy bueno, lo vimos en Hungría y Holanda", apuntaba. Pero la unidad de potencia flaquea y en Monza se apagó. No pudo salir al final de la Q1 y es otro golpe a ya un fin de semana difícil. "El motor no se encendía, así que tuvimos un problema con la unidad de potencia. No sé si es la cámara de combustión, la batería… pero sí, no arrancaba. Perdimos potencial en la qualy. Había algo más, sólo utilizamos un juego de neumáticos y el tiempo fue con el juego desgastado. Y después de esperar en el pit-lane mucho, ruedas viejas…", confesó. La historia del motor no ha cambiado y hasta parece desembocar en un discurso que al piloto le cansa repetir. "Tenemos un gran déficit en las rectas, perdemos todo. Los datos están ahí para todos, no estamos ciegos y son los mismos datos. Necesitamos la potencia, pero nos apoyamos y hay objetivos claros para el año que viene", admitió. En 2026 habrá algún lugar mejor... porque en Monza no. "Con Cadillac, nada más. Es un fin de semana difícil, Las Vegas será parecido… y quizá Bakú. Estas rectas exponen nuestras debilidades. Habrá fines de semana más divertidos, como Singapur, Austin… Y aprenderemos de los otros Grandes Premios y volveremos más fuertes el año que viene en las rectas", analizó. Por lo menos, la manejabilidad no fue mala. Aunque no era prioridad. "Aquí no hay mucha necesidad, vamos al 90% con el pedal a fondo. Sí que mejoró la manejabilidad, pero será más noticiable en Madrid o Singapur, lugares donde vas a tope en muchas zonas, pero en Monza necesitas más potencia que otra cosa", añadió. Su carrera queda comprometida. Aunque sí que servirá para el mejor homenaje a Adrián Campos. Y Alonso lo tiene claro: es una figura vital para entender todo lo demás. "Adrián Campos fue el que me llevó a los monoplazas y me dio la oportunidad cuando estaba en los karts. Después en el primer test con Minardi porque tenía una gran relación con Giancarlo Minardi… y así llegué a la F1. Si estoy aquí, es por Campos", cerró. El resto, como se suele decir, es historia.

articles.title: Haydock: Almeraq storms to brilliant Sprint Cup success for Haggas
articles.summary: Almeraq, Tom Marquand and William Haggas tasted Sprint Cup success at Haydock, with the Queen Elizabeth II Jubilee Stakes hero bouncing back from July Cup disappointment in some style.
articles.body:
Last year's winner Big Mojo flew out of the stalls and set the early pace alongside Marvelman, before the race began to get serious two furlongs out.

Paborus had travelled sweetly when he arrived on the scene - but as soon as Almeraq began to assert in the hands of regular pilot Tom Marquand it was all over, as the 9-4 favourite turned on the afterburners to leave the field in his wake, powering away for a four-and-a-quarter-length victory.

Victory completed a remarkable turnaround for the William Haggas-trained four-year-old, who suffered a horror fall in a sprint almost a year ago to the day which effectively ended the riding career of Jim Crowley.

"He has taken a lot of patching up from that fall at York, but to have him back in form and where he can do something like that is phenomenal," said winning jockey Marquand, who stood in for Crowley when Almeraq won the Queen Elizabeth II Jubile Stakes at Royal Ascot.

"Jim Crowley (who has taken out a training licence) has opened his next chapter which is extremely exciting and this horse opened his next chapter when he came back at Salisbury in the spring.

"That was pretty impressive stuff. We all really hoped that the ground was what let him down at Newmarket in the July Cup and he got away with it at Royal Ascot, but we are only playing an opinions game.

"But he is now a dual Group One winner already and is going from strength to strength. He is a hugely exciting horse to be in partnership with and awesome for the Shadwell team."

All roads point to the Qatar Racing British Champions Sprint at Ascot on October 17 for Almeraq, but Maureen Haggas, wife of the winning trainer, is hoping they might start mapping out some targets for next year as well.

"This was always his goal and then hopefully Champions Day, but hopefully he will stay in training next year, you would love to have him wouldn't you?" she said.

"That was pretty unbelievable today, but he does like the ground. I thought what he did at Royal Ascot was pretty phenomenal on ground that he doesn't really enjoy so now he has conditions in his favour and Tom knows him, it is exciting.

"He is a really talented horse and Ascot is the obvious place to go now."

Haggas himself was at Ascot, where he said: "I was thrilled to bits. He won here on the fast ground (Royal meeting), but he looked a good horse today on the slower ground.

"He settled well and picked up really well. He'll come back here for Champions Day."

Also at Ascot was long-standing Shadwell racing manager Angus Gold, who said: "Touch wood everything went well, he got the cover and the ground was to his liking.

"The gap came at the right time and off he went. He's beaten a couple of very good horses and it proves Newmarket was too bad to be true.

"Everything went as Tom wanted it to. He settled at the back, while at Newmarket he saw daylight and was too keen."

articles.title: Piastri es sancionado y los Ferrari suben sus opciones en Monza
articles.standfirst: Leclerc asciende al tercero en parrilla y Hamilton al cuarto
articles.summary: Leclerc asciende al tercero en parrilla y Hamilton al cuarto
articles.body: Oscar Piastri, tercer clasificado en la calificación del GP de Italia, ha sido penalizado con tres puestos en la parrilla de salida del domingo, por lo que deberá salir sexto. Los grandes beneficiados son los dos pilotos de Ferrari, Charles Leclerc y Lewis Hamilton, que ascienden así al tercero y el cuarto, respectivamente, en la formación final para salir en Monza. Las opciones de los dos coches rojos suben en casa, especialmente en una primera vuelta en la que suele haber muchas alternativas por efecto del rebufo... y este año de la entrega de energía eléctrica. Hamilton, que estaba especialmente defraudado, "pues esperaba estar en primera línea", asciende al cuarto y con más posibilidades de remontar y ganar en Italia con el 'cavallino' en el pecho, con lo que superaría además a Michael Schumacher en el trazado cercano a Milán. Hecho: El coche 81 obstaculizó al coche 30 en la curva 2. Infracción: Incumplimiento del artículo B4.1.1 del Reglamento de la FIA F1. Decisión: Descalificación de 3 posiciones en la parrilla para la próxima carrera en la que participe el piloto. Motivo: Los comisarios escucharon al piloto del coche 81 (Oscar Piastri), al piloto del coche 30 (Liam Lawson), a los representantes de los equipos y revisaron los datos del sistema de posicionamiento, vídeo, cronometraje, telemetría, radio del equipo y las pruebas de vídeo a bordo. Al salir de boxes, se le informó al piloto del coche 81: «Verstappen, Lawson y Sainz están cruzando. Sainz ha entrado en boxes. Solo están Verstappen y Lawson. Al salir de boxes, se le informó al piloto del coche 81: «Verstappen, Lawson y Sainz están cruzando. Sainz ha entrado en boxes. Solo están Verstappen y Lawson. Ten cuidado con ellos al incorporarte». El piloto del coche 81 declaró que no se le avisó de que VER y LAW estaban dando vueltas de empuje, pero se dio cuenta cuando estaba casi en la curva 1 de que VER estaba dando vueltas de empuje. Disminuyó considerablemente la velocidad y se mantuvo a la derecha para permitir el paso a VER, pero no pudo evitar obstaculizar a LAW, que venía justo detrás. Los comisarios aceptan que, con la información que tenía y la situación en la que se encontraba, el conductor del coche número 81 no tenía, en ese momento, otras opciones disponibles y, por lo tanto, obstaculizó inadvertidamente e innecesariamente al coche número 30. En consecuencia, se impone la sanción estándar de tres posiciones en la parrilla.

articles.title: Lewis Hamilton: Ferrari driver says team's execution of Italian GP qualifying could have been better after 'very tough' session
articles.summary: Lewis Hamilton almost dropped out in Q2 before going on to finish fifth fastest in Q3, which became fourth on the grid behind team-mate Charles Leclerc; watch the Italian Grand Prix live on Sunday at 2pm on Sky Sports F1, with build-up from 12.30pm
articles.body:
Ferrari had been tipped to contend for pole at their home Monza race but never truly appeared in the hunt at any stage of the knockout sessions with the Scuderia eventually outpaced in Q3 by three Mercedes-powered cars - including Alpine surprise polesitter Pierre Gasly.

Oscar Piastri's later three-place grid penalty means Charles Leclerc and Hamilton will still both start on the second row in third and fourth places respectively.

That final result could be viewed as fortunate given Ferrari's drivers had finished only ninth and 10th quickest in Q2, with Hamilton just avoiding a shock early exit at the hands of Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto by 0.001s.

Reflecting on how his session had gone in a qualifying dominated by drivers trying to ensure they had a slipstream-boosting 'tow' on track, fifth-fastest Hamilton told Sky Sports F1 : "It was definitely very, very tough, yes.

"The car felt really good in practice and in qualifying I didn't change anything, so I felt good going into Q1, and Q1 was solid.

"Then we sat and waited, and we waited very long in the pit lane for the first run of Q2, and for some reason we just didn't have the pace. I'm not really sure why, whether it was tyre pressures, tyre temperatures or whatever, so we need to look into that.

"Then execution in Q3 was pretty bad. I ended up out in the middle of nowhere with nobody, and then when you're following another car, you arrive several kilometres faster into a corner, so the braking distances adjust. It's all about getting into rhythm, and I got really out of rhythm for Q3, run one.

"Q3, run two, it wasn't a terrible lap but the references were all different, and we ultimately didn't maximise."

Third-placed Leclerc described qualifying as "a big struggle", pointing to "many issues in the background that we had to deal with".

Leclerc added: "I'm pretty sure if we speak in the paddock, everyone had some issues, because it's one of the most difficult tracks to optimise the power unit on. But that's not an excuse.

"Pierre and Alpine did everything perfect and I think they surprised everyone in the paddock by doing a perfect job. I'm very happy for Pierre by the way.

"Now it's our job to try and recover what we kind of lost on our own today. I don't think pole was possible but one place better was probably doable and we need to target on maximising everything and today we didn't."

Can Ferrari overcome Mercedes' straight strengths in race?

Despite their Saturday difficulties, Ferrari remain at the sharp end of Sunday's grid and therefore cannot be counted out of victory contention, although Mercedes' George Russell will likely remain favourite to win the race from second on the grid.

Ferrari have introduced an upgraded engine at Monza, which was expected to boost their victory chances, but Hamilton says Mercedes continue to hold an edge on straight-speed.

"I think we have a really great car," he said.

"It's all Mercedes engines up ahead of us and I think we've done a good job to be as close as we are to them, but they're ultimately gaining several tenths still on the straight. That is what it is, and so we have to just do the best we can.

"We're hoping for some tracks that don't maybe rely too much on power in the future, but I'm really grateful to the guys back at the factory because they did bring a upgrade here, they are really pushing. This is just the situation that we're in."

Leclerc hopes that potential differences in approach to energy deployment around the high-speed lap in the race could still offer up opportunities for the Scuderia amid expectations of a return to the 'yo-yo' racing of earlier in the season.

"On the straights, Mercedes are very strong. In the corners, we are very strong but we are going to be very exposed on the straights and to attack will be difficult," he said.

"But the deployment could make a huge difference one way or another and give us the opportunity to overtake. We will have to play it smart and see where we end up."

articles.title: Gasly, pole y venganza: "Llevaba esperando 10 años..."
articles.standfirst: El francés firma su primera pole en el mismo circuito donde ganó su primera carrera
articles.summary: El francés firma su primera pole en el mismo circuito donde ganó su primera carrera
articles.body: La historia más increíble de la temporada 2026 pertenece, de momento, a Pierre Gasly. Todavía pueden darse momentazos como el título más joven de la historia si Kimi Antonelli cierra su enorme campaña o una remontada desde atrás de Russell o Hamilton, pero esas son sólo hipótesis. Y en Monza llegó una realidad con un sonido estruendoso, el del público entregado a la brutal pole del francés de Alpine. Nadie contaba con él. Quizá sólo el propio piloto. De hecho, lo contó en sus declaraciones posteriores. "Llevo esperando 10 años para esto...", explicaba. Nueve van desde su debut. "Estoy tan feliz. Han sido nueve años, tratando de aprovechar cada oportunidad para conseguir esta oportunidad de la pole. Ganar en Monza y lograr mi primera pole aquí lo hace especial", añadía. Es su circuito mágico y todavía se recuerdan aquellas lágrimas a pie de podio cuando corría en Alpha Tauri. El Gasly del 2026 es diferente. Ya tuvo gloria en Mónaco, pero terminó perdiendo el podio en una sanción que primero fue anulada y después confirmada justo antes de inciar la acción en Italia. "Nos han robado", llegó a decir tras la brutal rajada de su jefe Flavio Briatore. Que ya ha llegado a ser desmentido tajantemente por la FIA y su Corte Internacional de Apelación. Pero ese mal rollo queda atrás... Porque el francés firmó su gran día y por sólo 60 milésimas desbancó al teórico favorito Russell. "Van nueve años en la Fórmula 1 en los que intento dar mi mejor nivel durante todos y cada uno de los fines de semana. Y no siempre tenemos el coche para pelear por la pole. Aquí fue el caso y estoy feliz y orgulloso de conseguir esa oportunidad", lanzó. Todo salió bien. "La vuelta fue una locura. Desde el primer momento en Q1 estábamos ahí y me sentía bien... Y después de nueve años esperando llega esta sensación", agregó. Volvía a su tiempo de espera y es normal. Fue una obra de arte. Y en carrera... pues ya se verá. "Es una pregunta para mañana", cerraba en la sala de prensa. Aunque sí, su coche está ahí, pero será duro y es algo que sabe. "¿Estoy en la mejor posición, no? Nadie sale por delante y me tengo que enfocar en mi conducción. Habrá ventajas en estar en cabeza, sé lo que se siente y es el mejor sitio para estar. Pero será una carrera larga. No tenemos el ritmo de los demás, pero hemos logrado mejorar desde el día anterior", concluyó.

articles.title: How Lewis Hamilton Helped Pierre Gasly Execute His Italian GP Pole
articles.summary: Pierre Gasly put his Alpine on pole out of nowhere in F1 Italian GP against the expectations, as George Russell looked favourite to start the session. The F1...
articles.body:
Pierre Gasly put his Alpine on pole out of nowhere in F1 Italian GP against the expectations, as George Russell looked favourite to start the session.

The F1 Italian GP weekend started on a sour note for Gasly after the FIA International Court of Appeal ruling, which took his Monaco GP podium and handed it back to Red Bull's Isack Hadjar. He was classified seventh eventually, as Alpine's Flavio Briatore unleashed in press conference .

Gasly sat out of FP1 for Paul Aron, to complete his mandated rookie session. But the Estonian did not disappoint to line-up 10th behind teammate Franco Colapinto. The Frenchman returned in FP2 to finish 14th after a time of 1m23.773s, while Colapinto was steady in 11th.

They felt reasonable after Friday, with the aim of a double Top 10 in qualifying in their usual position around P8-P10. The FP3 on Saturday did that for them after Gasly ended up ninth with a time of 1m22.898s, with Colapinto just behind him – both inside the Top 10.

Even then, there was no real pin on Alpine to do what they did by the end of F1 Italian GP qualifying. Even after Q1 when Gasly ended up P1 with a time of 1m22.612s, not many put him in the pole fight. He was up on Red Bull's Max Verstappen by 0.012s, while Colapinto was only 0.050s away.

The pace was unrelenting from Alpine and things started to get serious in Q2 when Gasly (1m22.077s) was fourth and Colapinto (1m22.400s) eighth. They managed to out-qualify both Ferrari cars in that session and were in the mix with Mercedes and McLaren at that stage.

While everyone was busy with tow and getting it right by playing games, Alpine went to their business without expecting pole. They were thinking to secure eighth and ninth at the very least ahead of Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad, after the second Red Bull of Liam Lawson was knocked out in Q2.

In Q3, Gasly was asked to stay behind McLaren's Oscar Piastri ahead on track. He put in a 1m22.001s to end up third after the first run. Despite being in the Top 3, the Frenchman complained that he lost a lot of time in Parabolica on the radio, meaning he had more time at hand.

The team said it could be due to deployment but it was nothing to worry about with the Top 3 at that juncture still a solid return. Gasly double checked on the radio if his upshift was right along with everything else and got a positive response from his race engineer.

The Frenchman was behind Russell and Piastri in the order after the first run in a close fight. For the second run, Gasly was behind Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton. It was a distant tow but the Frenchman made it with a 1m21.786s lap, enough to beat Russell by 0.060s margin.

Pierre Gasly's Radio Messages After Pole Confirmation

It was clear for Gasly that he got pole . No sooner that he crossed the line, Gasly asked his race engineer, "Come on, tell me?" And the response was what he wanted to hear, "That is pole"! It erupted with "what" all around, with celebrations from the mechanics echoed on the radio.

"Lets go!", continued Gasly, adding, "Been waiting for that one, nine years. F**k yes"! His race engineer applauded his effort, as the Frenchman continued his celebration. "Amazing, thank you everyone, very well managed. That was good. (inaudible) start, but I knew. Ooooh, nice, nice, nice, nice."

Teammate Colapinto was eighth with 1m22.220s. Crucially, he managed to beat McLaren's Lando Norris and constructors' rival Lindblad. For Gasly, it was a moment to cherish. He scored his first F1 win at Monza in difficult circumstances in 2020 with AlphaTauri. He has been waiting for 10 years since his debut to secure pole, with Abu Dhabi 2016 being his last in GP2 Series.

Interestingly, he scored a pole at Monza that year as well, when he secured the GP2 title with Prema Racing. Having had an F1 win, Gasly wanted to tick the pole box which he has finally achieved with Alpine. Naturally, there was lot of jubilation and relief. He is just grateful to have achieved the feat finally, especially with the French team at the receiving end of disappoint with lost podium.

He explained how the thought of F1 pole became real when he completed the first lap in Q3. The Alpine driver didn't think there was an inch that he left on track by the end of it. He put it down to perfect execution, even though the car didn't have that legs to secure pole unlike the top teams ahead. The update package from Zandvoort certainly helped, as he hopes to stick on, on Sunday.

Pierre Gasly's Reaction to His Incredible Pole Performance:

Gasly: "Yeah, I mean, I think… Quite a lot of emotions. No, I'm just extremely happy for the whole team. I'm extremely happy with our performance. It's been nine years I'm in Formula 1, trying to, you know, give my best absolutely every single weekend and it's not every time we get a car to fight for pole position. Today it was the case and, yeah, I'm really, really happy, really proud to have seized this chance and to make it work. It was a heck of a lap. We've been on it since the first lap in Q1, it's been feeling good. And, yeah, nine years waiting for that moment, that feeling. I got my first win here in Monza and now I get my first pole position, so definitely a special place to me.

"Today I was very lucky and I'm super grateful to have had the car that I had and gave me the chance. But, yeah, when I passed the line, honestly, it was the same as last time. I just shouted, I have no idea what I said, but I probably made absolutely no sense, I just screamed on the radio and just pure happiness, a lot of emotions, and extremely happy for my team. I mean, it's not my first race in F1.

"It's too many and I don't remember all of them. I don't know. It's definitely one of these laps that I'll put up there. I'm just happy, man. I'm just happy for the team and also, you know, the whole weekend, a lot of emotions, everything going on, etc. So just trying to stick at doing my job the best I can and that's what we did today. So very, very pleased and very proud of my team here."

Gasly: "It's been a long time. It's been a long time since I did a pole position. So, yeah, probably, I don't know, if you're Formula 2. So, yeah, Formula One is quite tough because you work as hard as you can to try to put your best performance out there and as I said, in nine years I was never really in a position to get a shot at it. I think the closest I got was in Qatar some years ago, but never really had the car that allowed me to fight up there.

"And today I think, to be fair, was probably the first time. And it's just such a nice feeling knowing that you are in the mix. All these last few hundredths you're going to squeeze out of that last lap potentially are going to be rewarded, because sometimes one of those laps, you know, will barely get us to Q3."

Gasly: "No, yeah, definitely not. I mean, Monza is a bit of a unique track. We know it, but, I mean, no, it definitely exceeded all our expectations. But since this morning, I think the pace has been better. We managed to make a good step, you know, from P3 to quali, and I think slightly bigger than the other guys around us. Yeah, straight from Q1, you know, we were a bit surprised to see us up there, as in mind, you know, our target was Q3. But then I think I was P1 in Q1, then P4 in Q2. I didn't want to get too excited, but then first run in Q3, I think I was third again and then I felt, "Okay, I really have a shot at it."

"And as I said, it's probably the first time I really get a true chance and, yeah, I tried to leave everything I had out there. It was quite hectic through Ascari and Parabolica. I don't think there was definitely much in there and, crossing the line, I knew it would be one of these laps that would be rewarded, but to the point to get the pole position, I didn't expect that. So, yeah, very, very pleased."

Gasly: "No, actually, I mean, didn't drive in P1. Yesterday in P2, things felt decent but for top 10. I think we made a few tweaks for P3, which again gave me a bit more confidence, and in practice I've never really had any tows. We knew that there was a bit more on the table in the practice sessions and then I think it was a very good execution from the team, you know, always putting me in a great position on track, managing the gap as best we could, really. So, I think my last lap, managed to target, slightly over 2.5 seconds behind Lewis when he was going to be fast and sort of, like, drag me with him.

"So, I think it was perfect execution. The car balance is probably one of the best I've had so far this year, really. Again, gave me the confidence to, you know, attack all these corners and sliding around and playing around with the car, and we managed to make it work in that last run when everything mattered. So, I think it's not down to, obviously, one simple parameter. I think everybody did a very good job and we've been rewarded for it."

Gasly: "Absolutely not. Yeah, I mean, the package brought us a lot of performance already in Zandvoort. We saw we were a lot more competitive and I think it's also, like, sort of giving me a little bit more what I need inside the car in terms of pushing my entries, being able to come into the corner, having a bit more consistent feeling with the car. No, the package definitely brought us good performance. Again, never imagined that we'd be in that position following Zandvoort."

Gasly: "I mean, I don't think I can say much about this and all I can say is it's not a nice situation, not ideal. Obviously, I try to use everything I can into something positive and, you know, extra motivation, but I think I could have dealt without it this weekend. Yeah, that's all I'll say."

Gasly: "I mean, it's going to be obviously great. I'm in the best position, right? I'm starting first, got no one ahead of me. I just got to focus on my driving and I know what it looks like having no one around this track, so that's a good advantage and probably the best place to do it. But then, yeah, it's going to be a long race. I think our— and I feel I actually felt quite good. Obviously not to the pace of these guys around us, but we seem to have picked up more pace from yesterday to today. So, you know, we'll obviously give our best shot and see what we can get out of it. But, yeah, I'm excited.

"That's a very good question. My plan is to stay first as long as I can. How long is that going to be? I have no idea. And my focus is going to be on my driving and making no mistakes and making the best out of what I have. So, I'm obviously really hoping we can stick, you know, to that position, but as we know, it's racing. Time will tell us and I'm just going to make sure I do my work as I always do, and Saturday night I come as prepared as I can tomorrow and give it my best chance."

articles.title: Riley Herbst confirms concussion sidelined him from Daytona
articles.summary: The 23XI Racing driver has been symptom-free all week
articles.body:
Riley Herbst confirmed it was a concussion that took him out of the seat last weekend at Daytona International Speedway last weekend.

The symptoms were the aftermath of a crash the week before at New Hampshire Motor Speedway when he crashed into the wall following contact from Michael McDowell. There was also a secondary contact when Connor Zilisch was unable to slow down in time and drilled into the 23XI Racing No. 35.

He had actually passed his concussion protocols in the middle of the week and even qualified last Friday at Daytona. However, he woke up on Race Day and felt unable to race.

"I got diagnosed with a concussion after the wreck in Loudon, and I thought that I was cleared to, to pass," Herbst said. "I passed all my tests the week leading up to Daytona. Obviously, I qualified in the race car, and had really fast speed, and then I woke up Saturday morning, feeling really, really rough with trouble with all the symptoms, the worst I've had since the wreck.

"So, I thought it was the best idea for me to step out and let Harrison (Burton) drive the race car, but back to being 100 percent."

On Thursday, Herbst announced he was moving to Legacy Motor Club next season, and spent time both in street car ride-alongs at Ten Tenths Motor Club and at the Toyota Racing Development simulator.

"We were at the sim, so I've been into sim every single day this week," Herbst said. "No symptoms, I've worked out every single day this week, no symptoms, and yeah, I did those little ride-alongs on Thursday with no symptoms, so obviously nobody knows until you hop in the race car, but I've been cleared of all activities and looking forward to completing another Southern 500."

Herbst felt fine immediately after the crash in Loudon but said his symptons have come and go so he won't be totally sure about the Southern 500 on Sunday until it's time to go.

"I don't really know," Herbst said. "They come and go. Concussions are a super weird health issue, health problem that honestly, it's an evolving matter. It's not like you can x-ray your arm and see a broken bone or see it not broken. It's all about how you feel in one day, you can feel 100 percent, and then I can wake up Saturday morning, like I did last week, and struggle to get out of bed.

"So, yeah, it was a rough process, but obviously I think myself, NASCAR, Atrium Health, we all did the right thing last week and taken me out of the race car for the betterment of myself and obviously the field of race car drivers, but you just kind of have to rest, rest, rest, and hopefully you can beat the symptoms sooner than you want."

articles.title: Mercedes boss Toto Wolff blames Max Verstappen for George Russell missing out on Italian GP pole to Pierre Gasly
articles.summary: George Russell missed out on pole as Pierre Gasly claimed a shock result for Alpine; Russell's final qualifying lap appeared to be compromised by Max Verstappen; watch the Italian Grand Prix live on Sunday at 2pm on Sky Sports F1, with build-up from 12.30pm
articles.body:
Russell appeared to be on course to live up to his status as pole favourite, but his final flying lap was compromised by Red Bull's Verstappen slowing down in front of him and his Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli.

Mercedes had placed championship leader Antonelli on track in front of Russell to give the Brit a tow, due to the fact the Italian is serving penalties for exceeding his engine-part allowance for the season and was going to start the race from the back of the grid regardless of his qualifying position.

Russell still improved his time to go fastest but then had pole remarkably snatched away from him by Alpine's Pierre Gasly, who pulled off one of the biggest qualifying shocks in the sport's history.

Asked by Sky Sports F1 whether something had gone wrong for Russell to miss out on pole, Wolff said: "Yeah, I think at the end where he got done over by Max in the final run when launching the lap.

"It was just much too close, and that compromised the lap time eventually and that lost pole position."

With having a tow from the car in front being crucial to delivering a fast lap at Monza, Verstappen sought to force another car in front after having lost touch with the McLarens ahead of him.

As Verstappen slowed down ahead of the final corner, Antonelli passed the Red Bull, while Russell remained just behind them.

While a tow is useful, being too close to the car in front for the entire lap can also have a negative impact on performance, which Russell felt was the case.

"We had a bit of a mess with Verstappen entering the lap," Russell said. "He wanted to go for the tow, Kimi was there as well, and I did my lap a second and a half behind Max, which wasn't ideal.

Asked whether Mercedes could have done anything differently to avoid the situation, Russell replied: "I think, no, everything was all looking fine, but then going into Parabolica, Max just slammed on the brakes, and he didn't want to be the lead car.

"So, it's just one of those things. You can't control what other people do. Kimi was there to give me the slipstream, which he did perfectly on the first run, but obviously with Max, I think it also made it difficult for Kimi to know what to do as well.

"So, it was just a little bit unfortunate. In hindsight, probably would have been better off not trying this, but we wanted to give it everything."

Despite his frustration at missing out on pole, Russell remains in with a strong chance of reducing his 59-point deficit to Antonelli at the top of the standings.

He told Sky Sports F1 : "I'm feeling good. I think the key is just to have a clean start, a clean first lap.

"As long as I'm in the top three or four after the first few laps, you're still within a great shot to fight for victory. That's the goal."

Verstappen: My car was jumping like a kangaroo

Verstappen didn't address the final-corner incident after qualifying, but revealed his own pace had been compromised by damage to his car, causing it to jump "like a kangaroo".

"As soon as I went out for qualifying, something failed again on the car," Verstappen told Sky Sports F1.

"It's something that we are aware of, and it happens more often in the year, but it's just costing lap time in the low-speed where the car just starts jumping around a lot more than it should do. On the bumps, the kerbs, the car's not compliant anymore.

"I was actually very happy with the car in FP3 because we took a big step forward from yesterday. The car was in a much better window, and overall I think today it was in a much better window, and overall I think today it was in a much better window.

"But when you have no ride control and the car is just jumping around like a kangaroo, you can't be consistent. It's actually a bit of a shame to not optimise our performance.

The four-time world champion qualified sixth but will move up a place to fifth on the grid due to Oscar Piastri being given a grid penalty for impeding.

On his prospects for the race, he added: "We need to be able to change whatever the part is, because otherwise it's going to be quite tough to race like that."

articles.title: Italian GP: Can Pierre Gasly win Monza race for Alpine just days after losing Monaco podium?
articles.summary: Pierre Gasly claimed a shock pole position just one day after losing his Monaco Grand Prix podium; Gasly starts alongside George Russell for what could be a thrilling race; watch the Italian Grand Prix live on Sunday at 2pm on Sky Sports F1, with build-up from 12.30pm
articles.body:
Just one day after the FIA International Court of Appeal reinstated Gasly's pit lane speeding penalties , the Alpine driver hit back with his maiden Formula 1 pole.

It is one of the biggest shocks in the history of F1 and, six years after winning his only race to date, also coming at Monza, Gasly has the opportunity to avenge, what he feels, was a wrong judgement call on Friday.

"It's been nine years I'm in Formula 1, trying to, give my best absolutely every single weekend and it's not every time we get a car to fight for pole position," said Gasly.

"Today it was the case and, yeah, I'm really, really happy, really proud to have seized this chance and to make it work. It was a heck of a lap."

Did 'extra motivation' power Gasly to pole?

Gasly has always shown plenty of emotion in and out of the car but was furious after finding out McLaren and Red Bull's appeals of the Monaco race result led to the return of his two five-second time penalties for speeding.

In June, Alpine had successfully won a right of review that saw the penalties removed as they proved Gasly was not speeding due to an incorrect measurement of the pit lane distance.

Gasly told Canal+ that "we're being robbed" and "I don't think this is going to end here" while Alpine chief Flavio Briatore questioned the relationship between the reigning constructors' champions and a judge at the FIA's International Court of Appeal (ICA).

The ICA responded to Briatore's comments on Saturday and stated they are "confident in the soundness of the proceedings and the integrity of the judges".

Nevertheless it certainly fired Gasly up and he produced one of the best laps in his nine-year F1 career, admitting the situation regarding the appeal was "not nice" but something he tried to use.

"I try to use everything I can into something positive and, extra motivation, but I think I could have dealt without it this weekend. That's all I'll say," he said.

Alpine managing director Steve Nielsen added to Sky Sports F1 : "When you think what the mood was in the camp when we got the result from Monaco, which honestly is going to annoy me for the rest of my life, it's a nice way to bounce back with pole position. It's lovely."

Several drivers congratulated Gasly on his pole, including George Russell who will start on the front row in Sunday's race.

Russell revealed he was playing chess with Gasly before qualifying and the Alpine driver also beat him in their game.

"We were actually finishing a game of chess about 15 minutes before qualifying and he beat me there, and I thought, 'Well, I think I'll beat you in qualifying,' and here we are, he's ahead of me again," he said.

"So, yeah, huge congrats to him. Pierre and Alpine have been super-fast even from Q1."

Gasly's only win so far in F1 came at the 2020 Italian Grand Prix - one year after his close friend Anthoine Hubert died and now he has another unexpected chance for a second victory.

The Alpine has been very quick in the straights in Monza thanks to the benefit of a Mercedes power unit, but the team also have a low-drag car which is strong aerodynamically.

Monza is an energy-rich track, so there is expected to be different power unit deployment strategies at play which will lead to the yoyo style of racing we saw earlier this year.

It may give Gasly a chance to keep Russell behind, or stick with him if the Mercedes driver is ahead.

Asked by Sky Sports F1 whether he could win, Gasly said: "Why not? I can be sure I'll do everything I can tonight, coming prepared for tomorrow.

"The good thing is, I know what it looks like not having anyone in front of you on this track, so at least if there is a place to start on pole, I'm glad it's here."

With championship leader Kimi Antonelli starting at the back due to grid penalties, a win for Russell would see him make significant inroads into his 59-point deficit to his Mercedes team-mate.

"It's going to be an interesting fight with Pierre as well. I think they've got a car that's got some good straight-line speed, which will be nice for them in the race," he said.

"I don't really know where the fight is tomorrow, but, confident I've got the pace to go for the win."
